rv.q: It’s hard to think when the Royal Court last staged a play that felt so dangerous, or one so spectacularly good.
Are we likely to see a more enthralling play in the West End this year? I very much doubt it.

What is really shocking and impressive about Nicholas Hytner's production is not that Dahl is exposed – this is a matter of public record. Instead, it's the fact that the play is a violent, incendiary provocation.
Giant shows a necessary bravery in taking it on.
Giant ultimately lacks tension, because it’s clear from the start that Dahl is deeply but lazily prejudiced, with no intention of changing.

For all the fine talk of separating the art from the artist, it’s hard to escape the discomforting conclusion that Dahl was so good at writing about hatefulness and cruelty precisely because he was, in some respects, a hateful and cruel man.
Giant is a far meatier reckoning with the invidious machinery of anti-Semitism than its own gesture of atonement.
Beloved American actor John Lithgow is terrific in conveying Dahl's charm and cruelty that are essentially two sides of the same coin.
